messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane Havili is a fifty-five-year-old Tongan-American man, divorced, who works as a live-in nanny for a family in suburban Portland. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his employer that he had not slept properly in months and had been found, on more than one occasion, sitting motionless in the kitchen in the early hours of the morning, unable to account for how long he had been there. His PCL-5 score of 65 places him in a range consistent with severe posttraumatic stress, and what emerges across intake and early sessions is a picture of a man whose grief and self-condemnation have become so thoroughly entangled that he can no longer tell them apart.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Tane's younger sister Lani was killed in a car accident in which he was the driver. They had been returning from a family celebration when another vehicle crossed the median. Tane survived with minor injuries. Lani, seated beside him, sustained catastrophic trauma to her head and upper body. Tane held her in the minutes before the ambulance arrived. He saw things — the specific configuration of her injuries, the stillness of her hands in his — that have since become inextricably lodged in his perceptual world. He remembers hearing her make a sound, a single exhalation, and then nothing. He has never been able to describe this sequence to anyone in full. When he tries, he says, the thread simply dissolves — he loses the order of events, loses the words, and finds himself stranded somewhere inside the memory without a way out. What he does not lose is the sound. It returns unbidden, most often at night, as a precise auditory echo, and when it does, the grief that follows is not gradual but total, arriving like pressure behind the sternum and staying for hours.

The triggers that now govern Tane's daily life are tightly organised around what he witnessed. Working as a nanny, he is embedded in a domestic world full of children's bodies — small arms lifted to be carried, bruised knees examined, the ordinary physical vulnerability of young lives in his care. On more than one occasion, the sight of a child's limb at an unexpected angle has stopped him mid-task, his vision narrowing to that single point of contact with the past. Conversations among the parents in the household about loss — a neighbour's bereavement, a news story about a family separated by tragedy — land on him with disproportionate force, pulling him back toward Lani before he has time to orient himself. These triggers do not merely recall the event; they confirm, in his experience, what he has come to believe about himself. He is certain he failed to protect his sister. He was the driver. He should have seen it coming, should have reacted faster, should have done something in those final seconds that he did not do. This belief — settled and immovable — colours every intrusion. When a memory surfaces and he hears that sound again, the grief it carries is inseparable from the verdict it seems to deliver: that he is weak, that he is less than a person, that he has been reduced by what happened to something functional but not fully human. He moves through the children's home performing care while feeling, underneath it, like an object executing tasks.

What makes the cycle particularly relentless is the way the appraisals and the memories feed each other. When Tane rehearses his failure — and he does, repeatedly, in the hollow hours before dawn — the memories become more vivid and more auditorily present, the sound sharpening, the grief intensifying. And when the grief arrives in full, it does not soften the self-judgment; it deepens it, as though the magnitude of his pain is simply further evidence of how badly he failed. The triggers, saturated now with this meaning, have multiplied rather than diminished over time.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when the youngest child in his care asked him why he was crying. He had not known he was. He is most afraid, he says, that he will never be able to explain to Lani's children — her two daughters — what happened that night. He is most hoping, though he says this quietly and without much conviction, that someone might help him find a way to finish the sentence.
